ways.name: Smithbrook Trail and the crest trail to Lake Valhalla
ways.season: Snow-free ground roughly July through October; the same slopes are skinned or snowshoed as a separate winter tour. The access road is unplowed in winter and typically melts out by early to mid summer.
ways.notes: From the Smithbrook Trailhead on the gravel spur off the highway, climb the signed Smithbrook Trail through nearly twenty short switchbacks to Union Gap, where it meets the crest trail; the summit is in view to the south for much of that stretch once the forest opens. Turn left and follow the crest trail south, contouring below the mountain's east flank through a mix of forest and open heather meadow and crossing Smith Brook, which is a reliable place to filter before leaving the trail. Where the trail bends away from Lake Valhalla, drop off it down a steep dirt path to the water and follow the rocky shoreline round to the lake's south tip.

ways.name: Crest trail north from Stevens Pass
ways.notes: Park in the north lot at Stevens Pass and pick up the crest trail heading north from behind the maintenance buildings. It contours the slopes above Nason Creek and reaches Lake Valhalla from the west, where you leave the trail and work around the lake to the scramble. It is a few miles longer than the Smithbrook start but needs no gravel road, and it is the usual start when Smith Brook road is under snow.

ways.name: Middle Fork Nooksack Road (FR-38) and Rankin Creek to the treeline camp, then the southwest basin
ways.season: Roughly Apr-Jun. A spring snow climb; essentially never done in summer, because what makes it climbable is continuous snow rather than the rubble underneath
ways.notes:
This is the more direct way to the X Couloir: from the south via the Middle Fork Nooksack River Road (FR-38). The southwest face can also be reached by a less direct line with more glacier travel; do not confuse either with the north-facing Coleman side, which leads to the other route on this mountain.

Drive FR-38 toward its mile-12.5 switchback and start walking the old decommissioned road around Point 4481 toward Rankin Creek. Snow travel — often by bike or snowshoe on the lower stretch — leads past East Rankin Lake near 5,120 ft and up into the basin to a sheltered camp at treeline around 6,100 ft, by the highest trees in the basin below Seward Peak. Roughly seven miles and 3,350 ft of gain to camp.

Access: FR-38, damaged in the December 2025 floods, has been closed to vehicles at milepost 7 by a washout since July 27, 2026, with no end date given on the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest alert still posted on September 26, 2026, and a separate gate at Wallace Creek near mile 10 closes the road 1 December to 15 June for elk calving. Confirm the drivable road-end with the Mount Baker Ranger District before the trip; the length of the approach varies year to year.

ways.name: Heliotrope Ridge and the Thunder Glacier cirque
ways.notes: Start at the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead and follow the trail toward the old cabin site, then rope up and cross the lower glaciers south into the Thunder Glacier cirque to reach the southwest side of the peak. It is less direct than the Rankin Creek line, with much more glacier travel, but it starts from a paved-to-gravel road that is usually open when the Middle Fork road is not.

ways.name: Bird Creek Meadows and Sunrise Camp, on the Yakama Reservation side
ways.season: Summer; non-tribal access to this side has historically been limited to a mid-summer to early-autumn window
ways.notes:
This is the southeast side of the mountain and the approach crosses Yakama Nation land, which makes it an access problem before it is a climbing problem. A tribal-use permit for Tract D is required, bought at the fee station on entry at the Mirror Lake gate — it cannot be obtained in advance — and it is only available when the area is open to non-tribal use. The Yakama Nation sets that window for non-members each year, somewhere between July and early autumn. The area has also been closed outright in some years, so confirm with the Yakama Nation before building a trip around this approach; there is no alternative way in from this side.

From the Bird Creek Meadows parking area (about 5,576–5,700 ft), the trail is easy to follow to roughly 6,700 ft. Above that it is route-finding: any number of lines through moraine, scree and glacier remnants lead up to Sunrise Camp at about 8,300 ft. Carry a map — locating the camp is the part people get wrong. Trailhead to camp is about 3–4 hours.

Sunrise Camp sits at the base of the Mazama Glacier, tucked between the glacier and a small rock hill, with hand-built rock shelters. It is a fine fair-weather camp and a poor one otherwise: it is exposed to winds that can reach hurricane strength, and to rockfall off the glacier. The rock walls help, but only somewhat.

From camp to summit is about 5 hours.

ways.name: Cold Springs and the Round the Mountain trail
ways.notes: From the Cold Springs trailhead, climb the South Climb trail to the Round the Mountain trail and follow it east across the lava flows to the reservation boundary and the edge of Bird Creek Meadows, then turn uphill onto the moraine toward the Mazama Glacier and Sunrise Camp. The turnoff is farther along the Round the Mountain trail than many descriptions suggest. A Recreation Pass is needed at Cold Springs.

ways.name: Start and finish at Killen Creek
ways.notes: Climb the Killen Creek trail to the crest trail and the Highline trail, then go around the east side of the mountain off trail, cross the untrailed gap on the Yakama side, and return along the Round the Mountain trail and the crest trail. The gap is open only a few weeks a year and needs glacier skills and route finding.

ways.name: Start and finish at Cold Springs
ways.notes: Start on the South Climb trail from Cold Springs and climb steeply toward Sunrise Camp, then circle the mountain mostly between 7,000 and 8,000 ft across many glaciers and moraines, picking up the Round the Mountain trail east of Horseshoe Meadows to return. It is a little shorter than the Killen Creek start.

ways.name: Heliotrope Ridge, the Hogsback and the Coleman-Roosevelt crossing
ways.notes:
Glacier Creek Road (FR 39) to the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead, then Trail 677 through old growth to the fork at about two miles. Take the right-hand climbers' path up the crest of the Hogsback moraine to the camps near 6,000 ft beside the Coleman Glacier, the same camp used for the Coleman-Deming and the North Ridge.

From camp the route ropes up and heads northeast, crossing the Coleman and then the Roosevelt Glacier. Expect two to three hours of glacier travel through a crevasse field before low-to-moderate snow ramps lead to the foot of the ridge.

ways.name: Artist Point and Ptarmigan Ridge to the Park Glacier
ways.notes: From Artist Point at the end of the Mount Baker Highway, take the Chain Lakes trail to the Ptarmigan Ridge junction and follow Ptarmigan Ridge west to Camp Kiser where the trail ends. Cross the Rainbow Glacier onto the Park Glacier and camp near the Portals, the usual base for the Cockscomb from this side. It is a much longer approach than Heliotrope Ridge.

ways.name: The south gully below the Carru-Lago col
ways.notes: Carru sits between Osceola and the higher Mount Lago and is almost always climbed as one summit of several on a multi-day trip out of the Harts Pass road end. Two lines reach the country below it: the shorter drops from Slate Pass and Buckskin Ridge into the Middle Fork Pasayten, then goes by Fred's Lake and over the ridge crest into upper Eureka Creek and Shellrock Basin; the Monument Creek trail is longer with more up and down. Tread through this wilderness is lightly maintained, with blowdown on the valley trail and stretches where the path is fainter on the ground than it looks on a map. The climb itself is short, well under two hours from the base, and unremarkable, essentially a heap of scree and talus with parallel ribs running up it.

ways.name: From Slate Pass down the Middle Fork Pasayten
ways.notes: The shorter and more common start. From Slate Pass the trail drops north to the Middle Fork Pasayten; follow it up-valley past the Berk Creek junction, then climb toward Fred's Lake and Shellrock Basin below Carru. Most parties combine Carru with Osceola and Lago over two or three days.

ways.name: Hannegan Pass, Easy Ridge and Perfect Pass, then south along the west side of the range to the Phantom-Crowder col
ways.notes:
From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead the trail climbs about 4 miles to Hannegan Pass, then drops the far side to the Chilliwack River. Ford the river near Easy Creek and climb steeply onto Easy Ridge, then follow its crest over Easy Peak. The Imperfect Impasse, a notch guarded by snow moats and wet, down-sloping slabs, usually has to be passed by dropping several hundred feet and climbing back up exposed class 4 ground. Beyond it, carry on to Perfect Pass.

From Perfect Pass the line stays on the west side of the range and heads south: across the edge of the Challenger Glacier, below Crooked Thumb and Ghost Peak, and along under the west side of Phantom Peak. Keep going south to the col between Phantom and Crowder. It is several days of travel each way, with no shortcut and no easy way out once you are past Easy Ridge.

ways.name: Baker River Trail and the Pioneer Ridge high route
ways.notes:
The seldom-used way in, from the west. From the Baker River Trailhead at the end of Baker Lake Road, take the Baker River Trail up the valley, then get up onto Pioneer Ridge and follow the high route along it to the southeast. Pioneer Ridge is a long, rough massif, walled by cliffs and slabs above the Baker River and Picket Creek, and its highest point is at the far southeast end, west of Goodell Creek. Crowder's southwest flank runs down at an easy angle to the foot of that ridge, so this line reaches the peak from below on the southwest rather than at the Phantom col.

Nothing about this line is recorded in detail: no mileage, no gain and no camps. Treat it as a serious cross-country route and plan it from the map. Baker Lake Road has been closed to vehicles and walkers from the Shannon Creek Bridge to the trailhead since mid-July 2026 for construction; check before going.

ways.name: Hoh River Trail to Glacier Meadows
ways.notes:
Hoh Rain Forest trailhead (about 578 ft) inside Olympic National Park. The Hoh River Trail runs east; the first ten and a half miles to Lewis Meadows are gentle old-growth walking beside the braided river, with water the whole way. Past the Olympus Guard Station the High Hoh Bridge crosses the gorge and the ground steepens. Elk Lake sits around mile 15 at 2,500 ft, and the trail then climbs in earnest to Glacier Meadows at 4,200-4,300 ft, about mile 17.2-17.5, which is the standard base camp.

About a quarter mile below Glacier Meadows the trail crosses a washout on a ladder of roughly 100 ft with a fixed rope beside it. For many parties that is the hardest part of the walk in.

In early season there are several steep, consequential snow slopes between Elk Lake and Glacier Meadows that want an axe and crampons.

A wilderness permit is required year-round for every overnight stay in Olympic National Park, obtained in advance through Recreation.gov or a Wilderness Information Center, and the Hoh is one of the areas that runs on a daily quota. Camping is not permitted between Glacier Meadows and the glacier.

ways.name: Glacier Meadows to the summit block via Snow Dome and Crystal Pass
ways.season: Late Jun-mid Aug for straightforward glacier travel
ways.notes:
Rope up at the toe of the Blue Glacier and travel up to Snow Dome around 6,600-6,800 ft. This is roped crevasse travel throughout. A large crevasse near Crystal Pass is often passable only on a snow bridge, and that bridge has to be scouted afresh each season.

Olympic National Park points climbers at the Crystal Pass line as the standard: from Snow Dome over Crystal Pass, then traversing immediately south of and below Five Fingers Ridge, over the false summit, and finally onto the true summit block of the West Peak. It is longer than the alternatives and generally regarded as the safer option through most of the season.

ways.name: Up the North Face to the summit pyramid
ways.notes: Most parties meet this ridge as the finish of a longer climb. Climb the North Face (or the Hanging Glacier or the Northwest Rib) to the upper mountain, then continue up the northeast ridge of the summit pyramid. A common way to the foot of the North Face is over Fisher Chimneys and down the White Salmon Glacier to a bivy at its base.

ways.name: From the Sulphide Glacier, across the Crystal Glacier
ways.notes: Climb the Sulphide Glacier to the base of the summit pyramid, then descend a short way east onto the Crystal Glacier and cross it to the foot of the ridge, avoiding a few small crevasses. The ridge is very loose fourth class until the last 200 ft, which is a solid, clean face of low fifth class leading almost to the summit.

ways.name: Mountaineer Creek to the basin, then west onto the Stuart Glacier
ways.season: Best while the couloir holds continuous snow and the steps take ice, roughly late spring into early summer; later the steps go rocky and the climbing turns mixed
ways.notes:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of Eightmile Road, follow the trail about three miles to the Colchuck Lake turnoff and continue past it for roughly another mile. Where the Stuart Lake trail switchbacks up and to the right, veer left to stay in the main valley — the same leaving point every north-side route on this mountain uses.

Follow the valley about a mile and a half to where it steepens, then turn right and work up the steep slope into the small hanging valley above, the flat basin under the Sherpa and Ice Cliff glaciers at roughly 5,400 ft. Standard camp is here.

From the basin the route continues west, round the far side of the North Ridge, onto the Stuart Glacier. Entry to the couloir is at about 7,800 ft.

The couloir itself runs 40-50 degree snow, narrows to a short steep step whose character depends entirely on the season, then a second shorter step, then opens into a wider snowfield leading to a notch in the West Ridge. Six pitches of mixed ground follow from that notch to the summit.

ways.name: Esmeralda, Ingalls Lake and Stuart Pass to Goat Pass
ways.notes: From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead, hike over Ingalls Pass to Ingalls Lake, then traverse toward Stuart Pass. Near 7,000 ft cross the scree gully north to Goat Pass at about 7,600 ft, where there is plenty of bivy ground. From the pass descend a short way onto the Stuart Glacier and traverse under the North Ridge to the couloir; the glacier passes above some large crevasses.

ways.name: Longmire, the Wonderland Trail and Indian Henry's Hunting Ground
ways.season: May through September; the lower cleaver is best while it still holds snow, since it becomes loose scree once bare
ways.notes:
Longmire (2,762 ft) is the start, on the Wonderland Trail toward Indian Henry's Hunting Ground. About 3 miles out the trail drops steeply to cross Kautz Creek — a braided glacial outwash channel whose crossing is periodically wrecked by debris flows off the Kautz Glacier. Ask at the Longmire wilderness desk before you leave, because a failed crossing means a long reroute rather than a wet foot.

Beyond Kautz Creek the trail switchbacks through old growth, fords Fisher's Hornpipe Creek and passes Devil's Dream camp (about 5 miles, reliable water) before opening into the meadows of Indian Henry's Hunting Ground at roughly 6.3–7 miles and 5,300 ft, marked by the 1915 patrol cabin.

At Indian Henry's leave the Wonderland for the Mirror Lakes spur — plank walkways over marshy meadow, then the end of maintained tread. The path fades into a boot track at about 5,600 ft in the basin between Copper Peak and Pyramid Peak. From there it is cross-country on the southwest and west slopes of Pyramid Peak, between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft, to Point 6631 just north of the peak. Snowmelt water is often available here into early summer, and the rock-slab camp below Pyramid Peak at about 6,300 ft is a common first night.

This is one of only two routes on Rainier that avoids significant glacier travel, which is its whole appeal; the cost is that it is long, loose and unfrequented, with about 12–13 miles and roughly 11,500 ft of gain to Point Success. Most parties take two days, often with a second camp dug into the cleaver crest around 10,700 ft.

ways.name: Kautz Creek Trail to Indian Henry's
ways.notes: From the Kautz Creek trailhead on the Longmire-Paradise road, follow Kautz Creek about a mile to a log-bridge crossing, then climb steeply through old growth and along the flank of Mount Ararat into the meadows of Indian Henry's Hunting Ground, about 5.75 miles and 3,000 ft. Shorter than the Longmire route but uphill nearly the whole way; from Indian Henry's the climb continues as from Longmire. The Kautz Creek crossing is periodically damaged by debris flows, so ask about its status before you go.

ways.name: Trail #1587 from US-2 to the Nason Ridge crest
ways.season: Late June to October; snow lingers
ways.notes: One of the steepest maintained trails near Stevens Pass, and it starts working immediately. From the dirt pullout on the north side of the highway the tread climbs on an old service road beneath powerlines, leaves the roadbed at a signed bend about a third of a mile up, and then runs into ninety-odd tight switchbacks on an open south-facing slope with no shade at all. Schilling Creek near the bottom is the only accessible water on the climb and it drops away quickly, so fill everything at the car and carry three litres or more. The grade eases into heather meadows around 2.8 miles and the tread tops out on the crest at about 6,000 ft.

ways.name: Snowy Creek trail from Smith Brook road
ways.notes: Drive Smith Brook road six miles and the narrow, brushy Snowy Creek road a further three and a half to a small trailhead with very limited parking. The trail follows Snowy Creek through old growth, then climbs to the crest and joins the main route about half a mile short of the summit. It is shorter and far less steep than the highway trail. The Snowy Creek road has been closed by storm damage since June 2026, so check before driving it.

ways.name: North Fork Entiat and the primitive Pyramid Creek Trail to the Emerald-Saska basin
ways.season: Mid-Jul-Sep once the col and summit gullies clear. October adds larch colour and early-snow risk; before mid-July carry an axe for lingering snow and ice
ways.notes: From the North Fork Entiat Trailhead at about 3,940 ft at the end of FR-5606, the first four miles of Trail #1437 climb gently up the valley through old burn, where blowdown and washed-out sections make the going slower than the grade suggests. There is little shade and the valley bottom runs hot and dry — carry water. Continue up-valley another four miles, gaining roughly 3,000 ft from the trailhead, to the Pyramid Creek / Fern Lake junction. That junction is anywhere from seven to nine miles in depending on how far up the road you were able to start. Fox Camp sits about a quarter mile north of it. From the junction take the primitive, unmaintained Pyramid Creek Trail west and climb about 1,000 ft over a mile to a mile and a half into the upper basin between Emerald and Saska, around 7,100 ft. The tread is intermittent. Pushing to that camp rather than stopping at the junction costs an extra hour on the approach day and returns about the same on summit day. This is reported as the easiest and shortest of the Saska / Emerald / Cardinal trio's summit scrambles.

ways.name: Lake Chelan: Lucerne and Emerald Park to Milham Pass
ways.notes: Take the boat up Lake Chelan to Lucerne, then climb the trail past the Domke Lake junction and up Emerald Park Creek to Emerald Park, about 6.5 miles, and on another two miles to Milham Pass. Drop from the pass into the basin between Emerald and Saska and pick up the south-slopes route there. A long, remote approach that suits parties already on the Lake Chelan side.

ways.name: SR-20 pullout, Burgundy Creek climbers' trail, the Bench, Burgundy Col
ways.notes:
Park at the broad pullout and overlook on SR-20 near milepost 165-166, about four miles east of Washington Pass, where a sign points toward Silver Star Mountain.

Drop down the embankment roughly 150 to 200 ft to Early Winters Creek and cross on a log. Logjams shift year to year, so scout up and down for the best crossing and be prepared to ford in high water or early season when the creek runs cold and fast with snowmelt. Treat this crossing as your last reliable water until camp.

On the far bank pick up the unofficial but well-defined climbers' trail that climbs the timbered rib on the west (left) side of the Burgundy Creek drainage. From there it climbs relentlessly and steeply through forest and brush for roughly 2,500-3,000 ft with almost no switchbacks and only fleeting water access early on. The tread erodes and is easy to lose in the timber.

ways.name: Silver Star Creek from the north
ways.notes: Park where SR-20 crosses Silver Star Creek and follow the trail up the east side of the creek for about two miles. Where it fades near 4,850 ft, trend west across the valley and climb open talus toward Burgundy Spire and onto the glacier. Best on continuous spring snow, when it makes a good ski or snowshoe approach; once the valley melts out it turns brushy and swampy and Burgundy Col is the better choice.

ways.name: Shannon Ridge and the Sulphide Glacier to the notch on the southeast ridge
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the Sulphide is walkable and the rock is out from under snow
ways.notes:
From the Shannon Ridge Trailhead, climb east-northeast up Shannon Ridge and onto the Sulphide Glacier — the standard Shuksan approach, and the same one the Sulphide Glacier route uses. Most parties camp on the large flat plateau around 6,400 ft, which is the usual staging point for summit day.

The snow between roughly 5,400 and 6,400 ft is where visibility bites: it is featureless open ground and parties report it as the tricky stretch in reduced visibility. Above camp the upper Sulphide is mellow, with a few small crevasses that are generally stepped over.

This route then leaves the standard finish. Where the Sulphide Glacier route walks to the foot of the summit pyramid and takes its Class 3-4 gully, this one gains the ridge at a notch further east and climbs about six pitches of well-featured 5.3 rock to the top.

ways.name: Lake Ann and the Fisher Chimneys to the summit pyramid
ways.notes:
From the Lake Ann Trailhead on SR 542, follow the whole Fisher Chimneys route to the foot of the summit pyramid: Lake Ann Trail #600 to the saddle, the climbers' path east to the chimneys, about 1,000 ft of class 3–4 scrambling through them, Winnie's Slide onto the Upper Curtis Glacier, then Hell's Highway onto the upper Sulphide Glacier.

Longer, steeper and more technical than the Shannon Ridge approach, and most parties take two or three days, camping at Lake Ann or above the chimneys. Where the Fisher Chimneys route finishes up the central gully, this one trends right off the glacier and takes the southeast ridge instead.

ways.name: Agnes Creek from High Bridge, into the Blue Glacier basin
ways.notes: From High Bridge, follow the Pacific Crest Trail and the Agnes Creek trail about nine to ten miles, cross Agnes Creek on a log and bushwhack steeply into the upper Blue basin, gaining about 5,000 ft. Camp on the exposed rock ridge above the Blue Glacier, directly below the east side of the Gunsight peaks.

ways.name: Downey Creek and the Chickamin Glacier
ways.notes: From the Downey Creek trailhead on the Suiattle River Road at about 1,400 ft, follow the Downey Creek and Bachelor Creek trails to Bachelor Meadows and Cub Pass, then go past Cub Lake, over Itswoot Pass and across the Dome Glacier to the Chickamin-Dome col. From the col, descend onto the heavily crevassed Chickamin Glacier and traverse it to the west side of the Gunsight peaks. This is a long, fully glaciated approach with a rope, crevasse gear and route-finding needed throughout.

ways.name: Over the pass at the head of the river road, then east and down to the lake
ways.season: Spring into early summer, while the couloir still holds continuous snow
ways.notes:
From the trailhead at the end of the river road, climb to the pass at about 5,392 ft - or to the nearby col used as an alternative when the pass is corniced - and then travel east, descending and traversing through the basin beyond, to the lake at about 4,170 ft, which sits just north-east of the peak. From the lake you boot or skin directly to the foot of the route, changing to crampons or ascent plates as the snow firms up higher.

This is the approach that suits the route's season: the couloir is a snow line, so the party wants it early, which is also when the pass is a straightforward snow climb rather than a scramble.

ways.name: From the valley on the east, reaching the lake basin from below
ways.season: Summer, once the valley trail is open and the basin is snow-free enough to walk
ways.notes:
The lake basin can also be reached from the valley to the east, which is entered by boat or floatplane and then by road and trail up the valley floor. This is the approach the other route on this peak uses, and it puts a party at the lake without any pass to cross.

Treat the detail of it with caution. The published descriptions of this peak disagree about which drainage is followed off the valley trail and how far the lake is from the road, and the two accounts cannot both be right - so plan this variant from current maps and imagery rather than from a written description, and expect the off-trail section to be unmarked and steep.
